note: S120f — predict-only, the signChart cluster. Every one of these lessons already builds a sign chart that clears manipulation, consequence and misconception; only the commitment was missing. Each wrong option is a documented confusion the chart itself can settle.

predict.prompt: f(x) = x³ − 12x, so f′(x) = 3(x + 2)(x − 2), which is negative between −2 and 2. On that stretch the graph of f is…
predict.reveal: Falling, and that is all it says. f′ < 0 is a statement about DIRECTION, never about height: at x = −1 this curve sits at +11 and is dropping fast. A chart of f′ can tell you the curve is going down; only a chart of f can tell you where it is.

predict.prompt: f″(x) = 6x is negative for x < 0. Over there the curve is bending downward. Can it be RISING at the same time?

options.label: Yes — bending and rising are separate questions
No — bending down means it must be falling
Only where f is above the axis

predict.reveal: Yes. At x = −3 this curve has f′ = 15 — climbing steeply — while f″ = −18 bends it downward: rising, but flattening as it rises. f′ answers 'which way', f″ answers 'which way is that changing'. Two charts, two questions, and neither one constrains the other.

predict.prompt: For f(x) = x⁴ − 4x³ the second derivative f″ = 12x(x − 2) is zero at x = 0 and x = 2. At those two places the curve…

options.label: Reaches a maximum or a minimum

predict.reveal: It changes its bend — these are inflection points. Maxima and minima come from f′, which here is 4x²(x − 3): a different set of places entirely. Three charts, three questions, and reading an answer off the wrong one is the most common way a sketch goes wrong.

predict.prompt: f′(x) = 3x(x − 4) holds one sign — negative — all the way from x = 0 to x = 4. Over that whole interval f will…

options.label: Fall the entire way, with no turn in between
Fall, then rise, then fall again

predict.reveal: Fall the whole way. A turn requires f′ to CHANGE sign, and inside an interval of the chart it does not change at all — that is what the cut marks are for. One sign, one behaviour: this is why a chart with three intervals is a complete description and not a sample.

predict.prompt: V′(x) = 12(x − 2)(x − 6) is zero at x = 2 and at x = 6. How many of those are real candidates for the largest box?

options.label: One — the other is not a box you could build
None — you need the second derivative first

predict.reveal: One. Cutting x = 6 from each corner of a 12-inch sheet removes the whole sheet — there is nothing left to fold, and the domain 0 < x < 6 excludes it. The algebra hands back two roots because algebra does not know what a box is. Checking the domain is not bookkeeping here; it deletes a root.

predict.prompt: A′(x) = 100 − 4x is a line with negative slope. Its sign chart will read…
predict.reveal: Positive then negative — so the area climbs, stops, and falls away: a maximum, established by the chart alone with no second derivative anywhere in sight. A line of negative slope crosses zero exactly once and only in that direction, which is why one critical point plus one sign change is already a complete argument.

predict.prompt: v(t) = 3(t − 1)(t − 3) is negative between t = 1 and t = 3. During that stretch the object is…

options.label: Moving backwards — which does not yet say anything about its speed

predict.reveal: Moving backwards, and that is a direction, not a verdict. Speeding up means v and a share a sign — so something travelling backwards and accelerating backwards is getting FASTER while its velocity is negative and still falling. Negative velocity and decreasing speed are different claims, and the sign chart keeps them apart.

predict.prompt: p(x) = x²(x − 4) is zero at x = 0 and at x = 4. The SIGN of p actually changes at…

options.label: Neither — a zero is where the sign is undecided

predict.reveal: Only at x = 4. The x² factor is a double root: the curve touches the axis at 0 and turns back, so the sign that arrives is the sign that leaves. Odd multiplicity crosses, even multiplicity bounces — which is why counting the zeros is not the same as counting the places the chart is cut.
